edits.rationale: The MongoDB tutorial says tlsCAFile verifies the certificate presented by the server. The Mongoose TLS docs say Atlas X.509 certificates are not root CA certificates, that passing one via tlsCAFile raises 'unable to get local issuer certificate', and that tlsCertificateKeyFile (a .pem holding client certificate and key) is the correct option. The 'not a mongosync incident' remark is the pack's own framing.

edits.old: A successful connection from one MongoDB client does not prove certificate compatibility with another. This is an adjacent diagnostic example, not a demonstrated mongosync failure. (high confidence)

edits.old: For self-managed X.509 client authentication, create a user in $external whose name is the certificate subject in RFC2253 form. Assign the migration permissions required on each endpoint; certificate authentication does not itself supply those roles. (high confidence)
edits.new: For self-managed X.509 client authentication, add the client certificate's subject (RFC2253-compatible) as a user in the $external database, and grant that user roles when creating it. The user specified in the mongosync connection string must have the required permissions on both the source and destination clusters. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/configure-x509-client-authentication.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/permissions.md

evidence.quote: you must first add the value of the `subject` from the client certificate as a MongoDB user to the `$external` database.
The RDNs in the `subject` string must be compatible with the [RFC2253](https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc2253.txt) standard.
The user specified in the `mongosync` connection string must have the required permissions on the source and destination clusters.
